chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz ibn Abdullah, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When the man from among you is asked about what he does not know, let him say, 'I don't know', and he should not say, 'God knows best', for that would cast a doubt in the heart of his companion. And when the questioned one says, 'I don't know', the questioner cannot accuse him.

key_terms.اللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ: God knows best — a common deferral phrase discouraged here as it can imply evasiveness
key_terms.شَكًّا: Doubt, suspicion — what is cast in the questioner's heart if 'God knows best' is used
key_terms.لَا أَدْرِي: I don't know — the correct and honest response to questions beyond one's knowledge

ai.seo_question: What should a Muslim say when asked about something he doesn't know?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) instructs that when a person is asked about something he does not know, he should plainly say 'I don't know' rather than saying 'God knows best.' The reason is that saying 'God knows best' can cast doubt in the questioner's heart — implying perhaps the speaker does know but is being evasive. The hadith also protects the one who admits ignorance from false accusation: once a person openly says 'I don't know,' the questioner has no grounds to accuse him of concealing knowledge.
